568.title: the golden deer
568.hook: something too beautiful to be real is grazing outside the hut, and only one of the three says so
568.howItsDone: The golden deer is a familiar scene in Ramayana painting and performance, and the phrase 'golden deer' is sometimes used for an attractive illusion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: threatened by his own king, Maricha agreed to go. Better to die by Rama's hand.

Near Panchavati, Maricha changes shape. Valmiki enjoys describing what he becomes: a golden body dotted with silver, horns tipped with jewels, a face of rubies and sapphires, ears like blue lotuses. It wanders near the hut, nibbling leaves, running a little, coming back, lying down nearby as if it had all the time in the world. The other deer of the forest smell something wrong and keep their distance. Sita, out picking flowers, doesn't.
screen: `GOLD, DOTTED WITH SILVER.` → `HORNS TIPPED WITH JEWELS.` → `THE REAL DEER KEEP AWAY.`

segments.voice: Sita calls to Rama and Lakshmana, amazed, and they come. Lakshmana looks for a moment and says it plainly. This is Maricha. Kings who came hunting in this forest have been killed by him in disguise. There's no deer like this anywhere on earth. It's a trick. Sita, the text says, is captivated. She asks Rama to catch it, alive if he can, so they can take it home to Ayodhya when the exile ends and keep it in the palace. If he can't, she says, bring back the golden skin. Rama is captivated too, but not naive. If it's real, he tells Lakshmana, it's a wonder worth having. If you're right and it's Maricha, it's a rakshasa who has killed people, and I should deal with it anyway. Either way, I'll go. Stay here and guard Sita. Don't leave her for a moment. Look how carefully the story sets this up. Nobody is foolish. Lakshmana sees through it. Rama has a reason for each possibility. Sita's wish is one anyone might have: a beautiful thing in a hard place. And still every reasonable choice walks straight into Ravana's plan. Valmiki blames no one yet. He just lets you watch the trap close.

569.title: the golden deer
569.hook: the deer leads Rama deeper and deeper into the forest, and with its last breath it speaks in his voice
569.carry: a voice in the wrong mouth
569.howItsDone: The golden deer's cry in Rama's voice is one of the best-known moments of the Ramayana, staged in Ramlila and retold in many languages as the turning point before Sita's abduction.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmana saw through the golden deer, Sita longed for it, and Rama went after it, telling Lakshmana not to leave her.

Rama takes his bow, buckles on his sword, and goes. The deer lets him get close, then bounds away. It vanishes into the trees, then appears again in a clearing, glowing, waiting. It runs, stops, looks back. Valmiki says it seemed to be playing with him: sometimes near, sometimes far, sometimes gone altogether. And every time it reappears, it's a little farther from the hut, from Sita, and from Lakshmana.
screen: `CLOSE, THEN GONE.` → `IT LOOKS BACK, WAITING.` → `FURTHER FROM THE HUT.`

segments.voice: At last Rama is tired, angry, and very far from home. He stops trying to catch it. He fits an arrow, blazing like a snake, the text says, and shoots. The arrow strikes the deer in the heart, and as it falls, the disguise falls away. On the ground lies Maricha, huge and bleeding, his real shape back. With his last breath he does the one thing left of Ravana's plan. He cries out in a perfect copy of Rama's voice: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! Then he dies. Standing over the body, Valmiki says, Rama is afraid. He remembers Lakshmana's words: it's Maricha, it's a trick. Now he sees the rest of it. If Sita hears that cry, what will she think? What will she make Lakshmana do? He turns and runs back toward Panchavati as fast as he can. Pause on Maricha. He warned his king, confessed his fear, and went only under threat of death. He dies by Rama's arrow, as he said he would. Many devotional tellings say that, dying at Rama's hand with Rama's name on his lips, Maricha was released. Valmiki just tells what happened: a voice in the forest, saying a name, in the wrong mouth.

570.title: the line
570.hook: everyone knows the scene where Lakshmana draws a line around the hut; Valmiki tells it differently
570.carry: let the forest be my witness
570.howItsDone: Reciters of Valmiki's Ramayana who pause on Sita's harsh words to Lakshmana explain them as words of terror for Rama, and Valmiki's Lakshmana leaves her in the care of the forest deities.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Rama's arrow struck the deer, and Maricha died crying out in Rama's voice. A voice in the wrong mouth.

In the version told on television and at bedtime, this is the moment of the line. Lakshmana, forced to leave, takes his arrow and draws a line in the earth around the hut. Don't cross it, he tells Sita, and nothing can harm you. The image is so familiar it has a name of its own. But open Valmiki's Ramayana here, read the scene line by line, and there is no line.
screen: `THE LINE IN THE EARTH.` → `DRAWN WITH AN ARROW.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO LINE.`

segments.voice: Here's what Valmiki does tell. The cry reaches the hut: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! Sita hears Rama's voice in pain, and she's terrified. Go, she tells Lakshmana. Your brother is calling for help. Lakshmana doesn't move. He's sure of two things: no one in the three worlds can defeat Rama, and Rama told him not to leave her. That voice, he says, is a rakshasa's trick. And Sita, frightened out of her mind, says terrible things. You want him to die. You followed us into the forest because you want me. Or you're working for Bharata. She says she will die before she lets anyone but Rama touch her. These are words of fear, and the text doesn't pretend otherwise. Lakshmana is shattered. Your words are like burning iron in my ears, he says. You are like a goddess to me; I can't answer you. Then he says this: let the spirits of this forest be my witnesses. May they protect you. That's the guard he leaves: not a line in the dust, but a call to the forest itself, and his own grief at being doubted. He bows and goes, looking back again and again. Where the line came from is tomorrow's story. Today is Valmiki's version: two people who love Rama, both terrified for him, and the trick working through their fear.

571.title: the line
571.hook: a line that isn't in the oldest text has become a word millions of people use every day
571.carry: some lines are there to protect
571.howItsDone: The Lakshman rekha is a common phrase in Hindi and Indian English for a limit not to be crossed, and the drawn line is a familiar scene in Ramlila performances and popular retellings.

segments.voice: Yesterday: in Valmiki there's no line. Wounded by Sita's frightened words, Lakshmana left her in the forest spirits' care. Let the forest be my witness.

Open an Indian newspaper and you may find it in a headline. A court warns the government not to cross the Lakshman rekha. A columnist says a joke crossed the Lakshman rekha. A parent tells a teenager: curfew is eleven, that's the Lakshman rekha. Lakshmana's line, a limit you must not cross, has become everyday speech. Yet in Valmiki's Ramayana, the line doesn't exist. So where did it come from?
screen: `A WORD IN THE HEADLINES.` → `A LIMIT YOU MUST NOT CROSS.` → `SO WHERE DID IT COME FROM?`

segments.voice: The Ramayana was never only one book. It was retold in Tamil, Bengali, Telugu, Hindi and other languages, in songs, plays, temple carvings and village performances. Each telling kept the bones of the story and added its own flesh. The line belongs to that later life. One well-known witness is Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, the retelling in Awadhi, an older form of Hindi. And here's a curious thing: even in Tulsidas, the line isn't drawn in the forest scene itself. It's mentioned later, by Ravana's wife, Mandodari, as she pleads with him before the war. You couldn't even cross the little line Rama's younger brother drew, she says. How will you face Rama? From hints like that, and from storytellers and folk tradition, the scene grew. Ramlila performers acted it out. Painters painted it. Television serials put it before huge audiences: Lakshmana drawing a glowing line with his arrow. None of this makes one telling right and another wrong. Hindus have long lived with many Ramayanas side by side. Valmiki gives Lakshmana's trust in the forest spirits; later tellings give a line in the dust. Both say the same thing: some boundaries are there to protect you, and danger comes when they're crossed.

572.title: the abduction
572.hook: a holy man at the door, a seat and water, and then a name
572.howItsDone: Hospitality is a Hindu ideal with old roots (the Taittiriya Upanishad's teaching atithi devo bhava asks that a guest be honored as a god), and tellers of the Ramayana do not blame Sita for welcoming the guest.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Valmiki has no line, later tellings drew one, and both say the same thing. Some lines are there to protect.

The hut at Panchavati is quiet. Rama is gone after the deer, Lakshmana gone after Rama. Then someone comes up the path: a wandering holy man. Valmiki dresses him carefully: a saffron robe, a tuft of hair, an umbrella, sandals, a staff and a water pot. Every detail says safe. Then the poet tells what the forest knows and Sita doesn't. The trees stop stirring. The wind drops. The Godavari, watching him, slows its current in fear. The holy man is Ravana.
screen: `THE HUT, QUIET.` → `A HOLY MAN ON THE PATH.` → `THE RIVER SLOWS IN FEAR.`

segments.voice: Sita does what a good forest household would do. She greets the guest, offers him a seat and water for his feet, and tells him there's food ready. In her world, a guest at the door is honored, a wandering ascetic most of all. He asks who she is, and she answers him straight: her father Janaka, her husband Rama, the exile, the brother-in-law, why they're here. She even asks his name. So the abduction begins with a kindness, and Valmiki never mocks her for it. Her goodness is real; the disguise is what's false. Then the mask slips. He names himself: Ravana, lord of Lanka, the one even the gods fear. He praises her beauty and offers her everything: palaces, servants, the place of his chief queen. Leave this forest, he says, and this man who has lost his kingdom. Sita is alone, and she does not flinch. She answers in a storm of images. Rama is a lion, and you're a jackal hoping for a lioness. He's the ocean; you're a trickle. Trying to take her is like pulling a tooth from a lion's mouth, or swallowing poison and hoping to walk away. She isn't bargaining. She's describing the size of his mistake. And words like that don't stop him. Valmiki doesn't pretend that courage always wins the scene.

573.title: the abduction
573.hook: carried into the sky, Sita turns the whole forest into witnesses
573.howItsDone: Ramlila performances stage the abduction, and tellings that follow Valmiki keep Sita's cries to the forest and its creatures.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a holy man at the door, a seat and water, and then a name, Ravana. Sita answered him: a lion and a jackal.

Words didn't stop him. Valmiki says Ravana's face changes, his eyes go red, and the holy man's body falls away like a costume. In its place stands the king of Lanka, huge and dark as a storm cloud. He seizes Sita, and his chariot, waiting out of sight, rises into the sky. Below, the hut gets smaller and smaller. Then Sita does something unexpected. She starts talking to the forest.
screen: `THE COSTUME FALLS AWAY.` → `A CHARIOT RISES.` → `SHE TALKS TO THE FOREST.`

segments.voice: Listen to who she calls. Rama, of course, and Lakshmana, the brother she drove away with cruel words; Valmiki doesn't stop to settle that, he lets it hang. Then she turns to everything around her: the flowering trees of Janasthana, the Godavari river, the spirits of the forest, the deer, the birds, anything alive that will still be there when Rama comes back. Tell him Ravana has taken Sita. It sounds like panic, and partly it is. But it's also a plan. Rama will come back to an empty hut with nobody human there to explain, so she makes the whole forest her witnesses. And she names him. Not just a demon took me, but Ravana. The message carries who, not only what. Later in the flight, Valmiki pulls the view wide: the river, the trees, the animals running beneath the chariot's shadow, and Sita in yellow silk against Ravana's dark shape, like lightning against a cloud. This isn't only a household's disaster; the poem wants the whole world to see it. But first, in a tall tree, Sita sees a bird she knows: an old vulture, half asleep in the branches. She calls his name.
screen: `SHE CALLS RAMA, AND LAKSHMANA.` · `THE TREES, THE RIVER, THE DEER.` · `A NAME IN THE MESSAGE: RAVANA.` · `LIGHTNING AGAINST A CLOUD.`

574.title: Jatayu
574.hook: an old vulture flies up at the most feared king in the world
574.howItsDone: Jatayu is honored across India as a model of loyalty; places in Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and elsewhere hold local traditions about where he fell, and storytellers often call him the first martyr of the Ramayana.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sita in the sky, like lightning against a cloud, calling on the trees and the river to tell Rama what happened.

He's old, and Valmiki is clear about it. Jatayu, king of the vultures, has lived a long time, and he was a friend of Rama's father, Dasharatha. When the brothers first came to Panchavati, he offered to watch over Sita whenever they were away. Now he wakes in his tree to her voice and sees a chariot overhead, with the most feared king in the world at the reins. He doesn't do the math. He flies up.
screen: `AN OLD VULTURE KING.` → `A FRIEND OF DASHARATHA.` → `HE FLIES UP.`

segments.voice: He talks before he fights, one king to another. I'm old, he tells Ravana, and you're young, armed, in a chariot, with a bow. Still, you won't carry her off while I'm alive. A king is supposed to protect other people's wives, not steal them. Put her down. Ravana doesn't. So the old bird fights, and Valmiki gives him a real fight, not a token one. Jatayu tears at Ravana with beak and talons. He breaks his bow, smashes the chariot, kills the beasts that pull it, and knocks the driver from his seat. For a moment Ravana stands on a wreck with Sita in his arms. Then he draws his sword and cuts off Jatayu's wings. The old king falls, and Ravana carries Sita on through the air. Remember what Jatayu said first: I'm old, and you're young and armed. He knew he'd lose. He fought because he'd said he would keep watch. And the first in the epic to fight Ravana for Sita isn't a prince or a soldier. It's an old bird keeping faith with his dead friend's son. Now the week. A golden deer too beautiful to be real. Rama chasing it, and a cry in his voice. The line, and Lakshmana leaving the hut. A holy man at the door, and Sita's lion and jackal. A chariot in the sky, a forest made into witnesses. And today, wings given for a promise.
screen: `I'M OLD; YOU WON'T TAKE HER.` · `BOW, CHARIOT, DRIVER: BROKEN.` · `HE KNEW HE'D LOSE.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `WINGS GIVEN FOR A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise you made that's still open; small is fine, like a call you said you'd make. Breathe in and hold it lightly; breathe out and notice how it feels to still be holding it. No planning, just let it sit with you, the way Jatayu sat in his tree, keeping watch.
Jatayu. The old vulture king, friend of Dasharatha, who fights Ravana in the sky to keep his word, and falls.
Your line: wings given for a promise. Tomorrow, Rama finds the old bird. Another week, done.
